title: Querying Big Data: Hive, HiveQL & the SQL-on-Hadoop Ecosystem
primer: The problem Hive solves. Hadoop stores huge data on HDFS and processes it with MapReduce (MR), but every MR job had to be a Java program, often 100+ lines for a simple GROUP BY. Analysts know SQL, not Java, so a simple question took days to answer (P1 slide 5). Facebook needed thousands of non-engineers to query petabytes.

Hive = SQL on top of Hadoop. Apache Hive (Facebook, 2008) gives you HiveQL, a SQL-like language. You write SELECT; Hive translates it into MapReduce jobs, Tez DAGs or Spark jobs (the "execution engine"). Analogy: you order food in your own language and the waiter (Hive) translates it into kitchen instructions (MR jobs) (P1 slide 5).

The parts of Hive. HiveServer2 accepts queries from clients (Beeline, JDBC, Tableau). The Driver parses, checks, plans and optimises the query. The Metastore is a normal relational database (MySQL/PostgreSQL) that stores table schemas, partition lists and HDFS file locations. The Execution Engine runs the jobs. HDFS holds the actual data: a table is a directory, a partition is a sub-directory (P1 slides 8-9).

Schema-on-read. A traditional database (MySQL) checks data when you INSERT it (schema-on-write) and rejects bad rows. Hive just copies files to HDFS and applies the schema only when you query. Loading is fast and flexible, but bad values show up silently as NULL at query time (P1 slides 13-14).

Partitioning and bucketing. Partitioning splits a table into HDFS sub-directories by a low-cardinality column such as date or country, so a query with WHERE on that column reads only the matching folders (partition pruning). Bucketing splits data further into a fixed number N of files using hash(column) % N, so two tables bucketed the same way on a join key can be joined bucket-by-bucket without a big shuffle (P1 slides 19-24).

Hive is batch, not interactive. HiveQL looks like SQL, but a COUNT(*) on 1 TB can take 5-10 minutes on MapReduce because MR writes intermediate results to disk between stages. Presto (Meta, 2013) keeps everything in an in-memory pipeline and answers in seconds. Use Hive for big ETL and nightly jobs, Presto/Trino or Spark SQL for dashboards and ad-hoc questions (P1 slides 17, 26).

The research and the case study. Thusoo et al. (VLDB 2009, ICDE 2010) describe Hive at Facebook: 2 PB, 15 TB/day growth, 7,500+ queries/day, 200+ analysts. Their most lasting idea is the Metastore, now the shared catalogue for Spark, Presto/Trino, Impala and AWS Glue (P2 slides 5-12). Spotify used HiveQL plus Spark, scheduled with Luigi, over ~3 billion events/day and 2 billion playlists to build Discover Weekly (P2 slides 14-18).

questions.q: In Hive, where is table schema metadata (column names, types, partition info) stored?
options: (b) Hive Metastore (relational DB such as MySQL)
questions.a:
Answer: (b) Hive Metastore (relational DB such as MySQL).

The Metastore is a relational database (MySQL or PostgreSQL) that stores table and column definitions, data types, partition values with their HDFS paths, SerDe info, statistics and privileges (P1 slide 10). Without it Hive cannot find or parse any table (P1 slide 11).

  • (a) Wrong: the NameNode stores HDFS block and file metadata (which blocks make up a file, where they live), not table schemas. This is the common distractor (P1 slide 28 instructor note).
  • (c) Wrong: HBase is a NoSQL column store for data, not Hive's catalogue.
  • (d) Wrong: ZooKeeper does coordination (locks, leader election), not schema storage.

questions.q: What does "schema-on-read" mean in the context of Hive?
options: (a) Schema is validated when data is inserted into the table
(b) Schema is applied when data is queried, not when it is stored on HDFS
(c) Schema is stored separately from data in HDFS metadata
(d) Schema is inferred automatically from column names in the file header
questions.a:
Answer: (b) Schema is applied when data is queried, not when it is stored on HDFS.

Hive copies raw files to HDFS as they are. The column types are only applied at SELECT time. A bad value (text "abc" in a DOUBLE column) is stored and comes back as NULL (P1 slide 13).

  • (a) Wrong: that is schema-on-write, how MySQL works.
  • (c) Wrong: the schema does live separately, but in the Metastore (a relational DB), not in HDFS metadata, and this sentence does not say when the schema is applied, which is the point of the term.
  • (d) Wrong: that is schema inference (like CSV auto-detect in Spark). In schema-on-read the user defines the schema explicitly with CREATE TABLE (P1 slide 28 instructor note).

questions.q: Which Hive optimization technique physically organises data into separate HDFS sub-directories by a column's value to avoid full table scans?
questions.a:
Answer: (c) Partitioning.

Partitioning stores each value of the partition column in its own HDFS sub-directory, e.g. /data/sales/year=2024/month=01/. A query with WHERE year=2024 AND month=1 reads only that folder and skips the rest (P1 slides 19-20).

  • (a) Wrong: bucketing splits data within a partition into files by hash. It cuts join cost but does not skip data at the directory level (P1 slide 29 instructor note).
  • (b) Wrong: Hive has no traditional B-tree indexes; it relies on partitions and buckets (P1 slide 16).
  • (d) Wrong: compression makes files smaller but does not split them into directories by value.

questions.q: Presto's primary performance advantage over Hive+MapReduce for interactive queries is:
options: (a) Presto supports more SQL functions than HiveQL
(b) Presto has better native integration with HBase and Cassandra
(c) Presto executes queries entirely in memory without writing intermediate results to disk
(d) Presto has native Python UDF support
questions.a:
Answer: (c) Presto executes queries entirely in memory without writing intermediate results to disk.

Hive+MR writes intermediate data to HDFS after the map phase and after the reduce phase of every stage. Presto streams data through an in-memory pipeline (split, stage, output). That cuts typical times from 5-15 minutes to 5-60 seconds (P1 slide 26). The key words are "intermediate results to disk" (P1 slide 29 instructor note).

  • (a) Wrong: the number of SQL functions does not decide speed.
  • (b) Wrong: Presto does have connectors (Cassandra, MySQL, Kafka, S3), but that is about reach, not speed.
  • (d) Wrong: UDF language support is not the source of its speed.

questions.q: HiveQL supports full ACID transactions on all table types, just like MySQL.
questions.a:
False.

Hive has only limited ACID support: UPDATE/DELETE work only on ORC tables created as ACID (transactional) tables, not on all tables (P1 slide 16).

Corrected: HiveQL supports ACID transactions only on ACID-enabled transactional ORC tables; MySQL supports them on all tables.

questions.q: Partitioning in Hive reduces query time by eliminating irrelevant data partitions from the HDFS scan.
questions.a:
True.

When the WHERE clause filters on the partition key, Hive reads only the matching sub-directories (partition pruning), so less data is read and the job is shorter (P1 slide 19).

questions.q: Hive directly executes a HiveQL query on HDFS without any intermediate translation step.
questions.a:
False.

The Driver parses the HiveQL into a syntax tree, checks it against the Metastore, builds a logical plan, optimises it and generates a physical plan of MapReduce/Tez/Spark jobs, which the execution engine runs (P1 slide 8).

Corrected: Hive compiles a HiveQL query into MapReduce, Tez or Spark jobs, and those jobs read HDFS.

questions.q: Bucketing in Hive is particularly useful for optimising JOIN operations between two large tables.
questions.a:
True.

If both tables are bucketed on the join key into the same number of buckets, Hive joins bucket i of one table with bucket i of the other (bucket map join), so no full sort-merge shuffle is needed (P1 slide 23).

questions.q: Explain the Hive architecture: what is the role of HiveServer2, the Driver, and the Metastore? How is a HiveQL query compiled into executable jobs? Draw the component diagram.
questions.a:
Definition. Hive is a data warehouse layer on Hadoop that turns SQL-like HiveQL queries into distributed jobs over files on HDFS (P1 slide 5).

Roles (P1 slide 8):

  • HiveServer2: the front door. A JDBC/ODBC server that authenticates users and accepts HiveQL from Beeline, BI tools (Tableau, Power BI) and JDBC drivers.
  • Driver: the brain. It runs the pipeline Parser, Semantic Analyser, Logical Planner, Query Optimizer, Physical Plan Generator, and manages the query's lifecycle.
  • Metastore: the catalogue. A relational DB (MySQL/PostgreSQL) holding table schemas, column types, partition info and HDFS file locations.
  • Execution Engine: MapReduce, Tez or Spark (SET hive.execution.engine=spark). HDFS holds the data: tables are directories, partitions are sub-directories.

Compilation steps (P2 slide 11):

  1. Parse: HiveQL text into an abstract syntax tree (AST).
  2. Semantic analysis: look up tables and columns in the Metastore, check types (e.g. user_id is BIGINT, dt is a partition column).
  3. Logical plan: Filter, Join, GroupBy, OrderBy operators.
  4. Optimise and build the physical plan: MR/Tez/Spark jobs, with partition pruning.
  5. Submit jobs to YARN in dependency order; results go to HDFS and back to the client.

Diagram (P1 slide 9):

   Beeline / JDBC / BI tool (Tableau)
                 |
                 v
            HiveServer2        (accepts query, authenticates)
                 |
                 v
     Driver: Parser -> Semantic Analyser -> Logical Planner
             -> Optimizer -> Physical Plan Generator
        |  schema lookup                  |  submit jobs
        v                                 v
   Metastore                       Execution Engine
   (MySQL/PostgreSQL)              (MR / Tez / Spark on YARN)
                                          |  read / write
                                          v
                                   HDFS (data files)

Example: SELECT country, COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY country becomes one MR job: mappers emit (country, 1), reducers sum per country.

questions.q: Differentiate between partitioning and bucketing in Hive. When would you choose each? Describe a scenario in Bangladesh e-commerce data where both are used together.
questions.a:
Definitions. Partitioning stores data in separate HDFS sub-directories by the value of a column (P1 slide 19). Bucketing splits each partition into a fixed number N of files, putting a row in file hash(column) % N (P1 slide 23).

PointPartitioningBucketing
Physical unitDirectory per valueFixed number of files
Decided byColumn valuehash(column) % N
Main benefitSkips data (partition pruning) for WHERE filtersFaster JOINs (bucket map join) and sampling
Good columnLow cardinality: date, country, region, statusHigh cardinality join key: user_id
RiskHigh-cardinality key creates millions of directories and overloads the NameNodeBoth tables need the same bucket count on the join key to get the benefit
DDLPARTITIONED BY (year INT, month INT)CLUSTERED BY (user_id) INTO 32 BUCKETS

Choose partitioning when queries usually filter on a column with few values (dates). Choose bucketing when you often join large tables on a key with many values, which you must never partition on (P1 slide 19: a 100 M user table would create 100 M directories).

Bangladesh scenario. A Daraz-style shop stores orders. Managers run daily sales reports by date and division (Dhaka, Chattogram...). Analysts join orders with a customer table on customer_id.

CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id BIGINT, customer_id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE
)
PARTITIONED BY (order_date STRING, division STRING)
CLUSTERED BY (customer_id) INTO 32 BUCKETS
STORED AS ORC;

A report for order_date='2026-10-01' AND division='Dhaka' reads one folder. A join with a customers table also bucketed on customer_id into 32 buckets joins bucket 0 with bucket 0, and so on, with no full shuffle.

questions.q: What is "schema-on-read"? What are its advantages and disadvantages compared to "schema-on-write" in a traditional RDBMS such as MySQL? Give one example where schema-on-read causes a data quality problem.
questions.a:
Definition. Schema-on-read means the table structure (columns and types) is applied when data is queried, not when it is loaded. Hive copies raw files to HDFS and only interprets them at SELECT time (P1 slide 13). Schema-on-write (MySQL) checks every row at INSERT time and rejects bad rows.

Advantages of schema-on-read (P1 slides 13-14):

  • Fast loading: a raw file copy to HDFS, no validation cost.
  • Flexible: load web logs before you know the final schema; no ETL needed at ingest.
  • Many schemas on the same data: define several Hive tables over the same files as needs change.
  • Open formats: ORC, Parquet, CSV, JSON, Avro.

Disadvantages:

  • Slower queries: data is parsed and checked on every query.
  • Bad data is silent: invalid values become NULL instead of raising an error.
  • Suited to OLAP (analysis), not OLTP like banking or e-commerce orders, where schema-on-write is better.

Data quality example (P1 slide 13). A bKash transaction file has abc in the amount column (declared DOUBLE). MySQL would reject the INSERT. Hive stores it, and the query returns NULL for that row. SUM(amount) then ignores it, so the revenue report is too low and nobody is warned. Fix: add downstream checks such as Great Expectations or dbt tests (P1 slide 14).

questions.q: Partitioning & Bucketing Design: You have a 5 TB e-commerce transaction table with columns: (txn_id, user_id, product_id, amount, country, txn_date). Design a complete partitioning and bucketing strategy to optimise: – Daily revenue reports filtered by country and txn_date – JOINs between this table and a 10 M-row user profile table (keyed on user_id). Write the complete CREATE TABLE DDL. Justify why you chose a specific number of buckets and which column(s) you partitioned on.
questions.a:
Step 1: pick partition columns. The reports filter on txn_date and country. Both have low cardinality (a few hundred or thousand days, a handful of countries), so they are safe partition keys (P1 slide 19). Never partition on user_id or txn_id: millions of directories would overload the NameNode.

Step 2: pick the bucket column. The join key is user_id, which has high cardinality. Bucket both tables on user_id with the same number of buckets so Hive can do a bucket map join (bucket i with bucket i, no full shuffle) (P1 slide 23). SORTED BY (user_id) also enables a sort-merge bucket join.

Step 3: size the buckets. Assumptions (state these in the exam): 3 years of data and 5 countries.

  • Partitions = 3 × 365 days × 5 countries = 1,095 × 5 = 5,475.
  • Data per partition = 5 TB / 5,475 ≈ 0.913 GB.
  • With 8 buckets: 0.913 GB / 8 ≈ 114 MB per file, close to one 128 MB HDFS block. Good.
  • With 32 buckets: about 28.5 MB per file: too many small files (5,475 × 32 = 175,200 files) for the NameNode.
  • Total files with 8 buckets: 5,475 × 8 = 43,800.
  • User table: 10 M rows × ~200 bytes ≈ 2 GB; 8 buckets ≈ 250 MB each.

So 8 buckets gives files near the block size on both sides, and the same count on both tables makes the bucket map join possible. If the data were bigger per day, raise the count (16, 32) keeping it equal or a multiple on both tables.

Step 4: DDL and queries.

-- Fact table: about 5 TB
CREATE TABLE transactions (
  txn_id      BIGINT,
  user_id     BIGINT,
  product_id  BIGINT,
  amount      DOUBLE
)
PARTITIONED BY (txn_date STRING, country STRING)
CLUSTERED BY (user_id) SORTED BY (user_id) INTO 8 BUCKETS
STORED AS ORC;

-- Dimension table: 10 M users, same key, same bucket count
CREATE TABLE user_profile (
  user_id   BIGINT,
  name      STRING,
  city      STRING,
  signup_dt DATE
)
CLUSTERED BY (user_id) SORTED BY (user_id) INTO 8 BUCKETS
STORED AS ORC;

-- Load with dynamic partitions (partition columns last)
SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition = true;
SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode = nonstrict;
INSERT INTO transactions PARTITION (txn_date, country)
SELECT txn_id, user_id, product_id, amount, txn_date, country
FROM raw_transactions;

-- Daily report: reads one directory
SELECT SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM transactions
WHERE txn_date = '2024-10-01' AND country = 'BD';

-- Join: bucket i with bucket i
SET hive.optimize.bucketmapjoin = true;
SET hive.optimize.bucketmapjoin.sortedmerge = true;
SELECT u.city, SUM(t.amount)
FROM transactions t JOIN user_profile u ON t.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE t.txn_date = '2024-10-01'
GROUP BY u.city;

Effect. A daily report for one country reads one partition, about 1/5,475 of the table (about 0.018%) instead of 5 TB. The join reads matching bucket pairs instead of shuffling both tables. Note: partition columns are not repeated in the column list, and must come last in a dynamic partition INSERT (P1 slide 22).

questions.q: Query Compilation to MapReduce: Write HiveQL to find the top 5 products by total revenue in 2023. Then trace how Hive compiles this query into MapReduce stages: what is emitted by the Map phase, what is the shuffle key, and what does the Reduce phase compute? How would switching the execution engine from MapReduce to Tez change the execution plan?
questions.a:
Step 1: HiveQL (same style as P1 slide 18):

SELECT   product_id,
         SUM(amount) AS total_revenue
FROM     transactions
WHERE    YEAR(txn_date) = 2023
GROUP BY product_id
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
LIMIT    5;

Step 2: compilation (P1 slide 8, P2 slide 11). Parse to AST; semantic analysis checks transactions, product_id, amount, txn_date in the Metastore; logical plan = Filter, GroupBy, OrderBy, Limit; physical plan = two MR jobs.

Job 1: aggregate.

  • Map: read each row (or only the 2023 partitions if the table is partitioned by date), drop rows where YEAR(txn_date) is not 2023, emit (product_id, amount). Hive does map-side aggregation (a combiner): each mapper emits one partial sum per product (P2 slide 10).
  • Shuffle key: product_id. All partial sums for one product go to the same reducer.
  • Reduce: add the partial sums: (product_id, SUM(amount)). Output is written to a temporary HDFS file.

Job 2: sort and limit.

  • Map: read Job 1 output, emit (total_revenue, product_id); each mapper can keep only its own top 5 (limit push-down).
  • Shuffle key: total_revenue in descending order, all to one reducer because ORDER BY needs a global order.
  • Reduce: output the first 5 rows.

Tiny example. 2023 rows: (P1,100), (P2,50), (P1,30), (P3,80), (P2,20), (P4,10). Job 1 gives P1=130, P2=70, P3=80, P4=10. Job 2 sorts: P1 130, P3 80, P2 70, P4 10 (all 4 shown since fewer than 5).

Step 3: MapReduce vs Tez. With SET hive.execution.engine=tez the two jobs become one DAG: Map 1 (scan, filter, partial sum) to Reducer 2 (final sum) to Reducer 3 (sort, limit 5). Differences:

  • No HDFS write between Job 1 and Job 2: data passes directly between stages.
  • One job submission instead of two, and containers can be reused, so less start-up cost.
  • Same HiveQL, same result; only the plan and speed change (Tez is "DAG of tasks, faster", P1 slide 8).

questions.q: Spotify's co-occurrence query runs GROUP BY song_a, song_b over 2 billion playlist rows. Estimate the output size if there are 30M songs. Propose a partitioning + bucketing scheme for the playlist_songs Hive table that would reduce the shuffle size for this query. [CLO4 – Apply]
questions.a:
What the query does. For every playlist, every pair of songs in it is one row; GROUP BY counts how many playlists contain each pair; HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 keeps frequent pairs (P2 slide 16).

Estimate 1: upper bound from the song count. Possible distinct pairs = 30M × (30M − 1) / 2 ≈ 4.5 × 10^14. At 16 bytes per output row (two 4-byte song ids + 8-byte count) that is about 7.2 PB. This can never happen in practice, because pairs only come from real playlists.

Estimate 2: from the data. Assume the 2 billion rows are (playlist, song) rows and a playlist has about 20 songs on average.

  • Playlists = 2 × 10^9 / 20 = 10^8 (100 million).
  • Pairs per playlist = 20 × 19 / 2 = 190.
  • Pair rows before GROUP BY = 10^8 × 190 = 1.9 × 10^10 (19 billion).
  • Distinct pairs are at most 1.9 × 10^10, which is about 0.0042% of the 4.5 × 10^14 possible pairs; at 16 bytes that is at most about 304 GB.
  • After HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 most pairs vanish (the long tail), so the final output is far smaller, likely a few GB.

(If instead there are 2 billion playlists of 20 songs, the pair rows are 2 × 10^9 × 190 = 3.8 × 10^11, about 6.08 TB at 16 bytes. Show your assumption.)

Where the shuffle comes from. (1) The self-join on playlist_id to build pairs, which shuffles all 2B rows by playlist. (2) The GROUP BY on (song_a, song_b), which shuffles the pairs.

Proposed scheme:

CREATE TABLE playlist_songs (
  playlist_id BIGINT,
  song_id     INT,
  added_ts    TIMESTAMP
)
PARTITIONED BY (week STRING)
CLUSTERED BY (playlist_id) SORTED BY (playlist_id, song_id)
INTO 1024 BUCKETS
STORED AS ORC;
  • Partition by week: the weekly job reads only new or changed weeks. The slides report that partitioning play_events by week cut the query from 8 hours to 2 hours, a 4× speed-up (P2 slide 18).
  • Bucket by playlist_id: all songs of one playlist sit in one bucket file, so the self-join is done inside each bucket with no shuffle. Sorting by (playlist_id, song_id) gives a sort-merge bucket join and makes a.song_id < b.song_id pairs easy to generate.
  • Map-side aggregation on (song_a, song_b) shrinks the second shuffle, the same trick that cut shuffle data about 250,000× for GROUP BY country (P2 slide 10).
  • Do not partition by song_id or playlist_id: 30M or 100M+ directories would crash the NameNode (P1 slide 19).

Other side. Bucketing by playlist_id does not help the GROUP BY shuffle itself, because the group key is the song pair. An option is to precompute and store the weekly pair counts and add each new week incrementally (Luigi skips finished outputs, P2 slide 14).

questions.q: The ALS collaborative filtering model is a matrix factorisation over a 75M-user × 30M-song matrix. At 4 bytes per float and rank k = 50, calculate the model size and explain whether it fits in a 5,000-node YARN cluster's aggregate RAM. [CLO4 – Analyse]
questions.a:
Idea. ALS (Alternating Least Squares) does not store the full user × song matrix. It learns two small matrices: a user matrix U (one row of k numbers per user) and a song matrix V (one row of k numbers per song). A user's predicted liking for a song = dot product of their two rows. Analogy: describe each person and each song by 50 "taste" scores instead of storing every person-song rating.

Calculation.

  • User factors: 75 × 10^6 × 50 × 4 B = 1.5 × 10^10 B = 15 GB.
  • Song factors: 30 × 10^6 × 50 × 4 B = 6 × 10^9 B = 6 GB.
  • Model size = (75M + 30M) × 50 × 4 B = 2.1 × 10^10 B = 21 GB (about 19.6 GiB).

Compare with the full matrix. 75M × 30M × 4 B = 9 × 10^15 B = 9 PB. Factorisation makes the model about 430,000 times smaller (9 × 10^15 / 2.1 × 10^10).

Does it fit? The slides do not give RAM per node. Assume 64 GB per node: aggregate RAM = 5,000 × 64 GB = 320 TB. 21 GB is about 0.0066% of that. Even split evenly it is about 4.2 MB per node. So yes, it fits easily; it would even fit in one large server's memory. The dense 9 PB matrix would not fit (about 28 times the 320 TB).

Caveats. Training needs more than the model: the rating/interaction data, shuffled factor blocks each iteration, and JVM overhead, often several times the model size. Spark ALS partitions U and V into blocks across executors so each node holds only a slice. Still well within the cluster.

questions.q: Spotify uses Luigi while other companies use Apache Airflow. Compare the two on: dependency declaration style, backfill capability, and UI/observability. Which would you choose for a 100-step daily pipeline? [CLO3 – Evaluate]
questions.a:
Background. Both are Python workflow schedulers: they run many jobs (HiveQL, Spark) in the right order. Luigi was open-sourced by Spotify in 2012. A Luigi task declares its output (an HDFS path) and its input dependencies (other tasks), and Luigi skips tasks whose output already exists (P2 slide 14). Airflow (from Airbnb, now Apache) is general knowledge, not on the slides.

AspectLuigiAirflow
Dependency styleTarget-based and pull: each Task class has requires(), output(), run(). You ask for the final task; Luigi walks back through requirements and runs only what is missing.DAG-based and push: a DAG file lists tasks (operators) and edges (t1 >> t2). The scheduler runs the DAG on a timetable.
BackfillRe-run for past dates by passing date parameters (or range tasks); idempotent because finished outputs are skipped. No built-in scheduler: usually triggered by cron.Built in: each run has a logical date; catchup and airflow dags backfill run missed dates; per-task retries and clearing.
UI / observabilitySimple central-scheduler web page showing task status and the dependency graph.Rich web UI: grid and graph views, per-task logs, run history, retries, SLAs and alerting.

Choice for a 100-step daily pipeline: Airflow. With 100 steps you need a clear view of which step failed, its logs, automatic retries, alerts, and an easy way to re-run past days. Airflow gives these out of the box.

Other side. Luigi is lighter and its "skip if output exists" model is a natural fit for file-based Hadoop pipelines like Spotify's, where it enabled incremental daily runs (P2 slide 14). A small team already using Luigi might keep it. But at 100 steps the monitoring and backfill tooling of Airflow outweighs that.

questions.q: Task (25 minutes, pairs): Simulate a Hive session using PySpark's SQL interface (which reads the same Hive Metastore). Dataset: a 10,000-row synthetic play_events CSV (generate with the skeleton below).
questions.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
import random, datetime

spark = SparkSession.builder \
        .appName("HiveDemo") \
        .getOrCreate()
spark.setLogLevel("WARN")

# Generate synthetic data
rows = []
for i in range(10_000):
    rows.append({
      "user_id":    random.randint(1, 500),
      "song_id":    random.randint(1, 200),
      "playlist_id":random.randint(1, 1000),
      "dt":         "2024-10-01"
    })

df = spark.createDataFrame(rows)
df.createOrReplaceTempView("play_events")

# Co-occurrence query
result = spark.sql("""
    SELECT a.song_id AS song_a,
           b.song_id AS song_b,
           COUNT(*) AS co_count
    FROM play_events a
    JOIN play_events b
      ON a.playlist_id = b.playlist_id
     AND a.song_id < b.song_id
    GROUP BY a.song_id, b.song_id
    HAVING COUNT(*) > 2
    ORDER BY co_count DESC
""")
result.show(10)
questions.a:
What the skeleton does. It builds 10,000 random rows (user 1-500, song 1-200, playlist 1-1000, all on dt 2024-10-01), registers them as a temporary view play_events, then runs the Spotify-style co-occurrence query: a self-join on playlist_id makes every pair of songs in the same playlist, a.song_id < b.song_id keeps each pair once and drops a song paired with itself, GROUP BY counts the pairs, HAVING keeps pairs seen more than 2 times (P2 slide 16 uses > 5 at Spotify scale).

Steps.

  1. Install PySpark (pip install pyspark) or open pyspark on the lab Hadoop machine.
  2. Save the complete script below as live_w07.py and run spark-submit live_w07.py.
  3. Read the printed tables, timings and plans, and answer Goals 1-4.

Complete script (expected to run; not run here). Changes from the skeleton: fixed random seed, two dates so pruning shows up, timing, the songs table, and EXPLAIN. datetime from the skeleton is unused and dropped.

# live_w07.py  -- run with: spark-submit live_w07.py   (or paste into pyspark)
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
import random, time

spark = SparkSession.builder \
        .appName("HiveDemo") \
        .getOrCreate()
spark.setLogLevel("WARN")

# ---- Generate synthetic data (two dates so pruning is visible) ----
random.seed(42)
rows = []
for i in range(10_000):
    rows.append({
      "user_id":     random.randint(1, 500),
      "song_id":     random.randint(1, 200),
      "playlist_id": random.randint(1, 1000),
      "dt":          random.choice(["2024-10-01", "2024-10-02"])
    })
df = spark.createDataFrame(rows)

# ---- Goal 1: partitioned table on dt ----
spark.sql("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS play_events_part")
(df.write.mode("overwrite")
   .partitionBy("dt")
   .format("parquet")
   .saveAsTable("play_events_part"))
spark.sql("SHOW PARTITIONS play_events_part").show()

# ---- Goal 2: co-occurrence query, timed ----
cooc_sql = """
    SELECT a.song_id AS song_a,
           b.song_id AS song_b,
           COUNT(*) AS co_count
    FROM play_events_part a
    JOIN play_events_part b
      ON a.playlist_id = b.playlist_id
     AND a.song_id < b.song_id
    WHERE a.dt = '2024-10-01' AND b.dt = '2024-10-01'
    GROUP BY a.song_id, b.song_id
    HAVING COUNT(*) > 2
    ORDER BY co_count DESC
"""
t0 = time.time()
result = spark.sql(cooc_sql)
result.show(10)
print("rows kept:", result.count())
print("co-occurrence time: %.2f s" % (time.time() - t0))

# ---- Goal 3: songs dimension table + broadcast hint ----
genres = ["pop", "rock", "baul", "rabindra", "hiphop"]
songs = spark.createDataFrame(
    [(s, "Song %d" % s, random.choice(genres)) for s in range(1, 201)],
    ["song_id", "title", "genre"])
songs.createOrReplaceTempView("songs")

plain_sql = """
    SELECT s.genre, COUNT(*) AS plays
    FROM play_events_part p JOIN songs s ON p.song_id = s.song_id
    WHERE p.dt = '2024-10-01'
    GROUP BY s.genre
"""
hint_sql = """
    SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(s) */ s.genre, COUNT(*) AS plays
    FROM play_events_part p JOIN songs s ON p.song_id = s.song_id
    WHERE p.dt = '2024-10-01'
    GROUP BY s.genre
"""
# turn off automatic broadcast so the comparison is fair
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", -1)
t0 = time.time(); spark.sql(plain_sql).collect(); t_plain = time.time() - t0
t0 = time.time(); spark.sql(hint_sql).collect();  t_hint  = time.time() - t0
print("no hint: %.2f s   broadcast hint: %.2f s" % (t_plain, t_hint))

# ---- Goal 4: EXPLAIN, find partition pruning ----
spark.sql("EXPLAIN FORMATTED " + hint_sql).show(truncate=False)
spark.sql(hint_sql).explain(mode="formatted")

spark.stop()

Expected output size (from a Python simulation of the same random data, 20 seeds, using the skeleton's single date). Each playlist gets about 10,000 / 1,000 = 10 rows, so the join produces about 50,000 pair rows; these fall into about 18,000 distinct song pairs out of 200 × 199 / 2 = 19,900 possible; about 9,000 pairs pass HAVING COUNT(*) > 2; the top co_count is about 11-13. With the full script's two dates, the day-1 filter keeps about half the rows (about 5 per playlist), so the counts are much smaller and fewer pairs pass. Exact numbers change with the random data.

questions.q: Create a partitioned Spark table (partition on dt).
questions.a:
df.write.partitionBy("dt").saveAsTable("play_events_part") writes one sub-directory per date under the warehouse folder: spark-warehouse/play_events_part/dt=2024-10-01/ and dt=2024-10-02/, the same layout as Hive's year=2024/month=01/ (P1 slide 20). The table and its partitions are registered in the catalogue (the Metastore if Spark is built with Hive support, otherwise Spark's own catalogue). Expected SHOW PARTITIONS output: two rows, dt=2024-10-01 and dt=2024-10-02.

Hive equivalent: CREATE TABLE play_events (user_id INT, song_id INT, playlist_id INT) PARTITIONED BY (dt STRING) STORED AS ORC; plus a dynamic partition INSERT with dt last in the SELECT (P1 slide 22).

questions.q: Run the co-occurrence query and time it.
questions.a:
Wrap the query in time.time() calls. Call an action (show, count, collect): Spark is lazy (Week 6), so spark.sql() alone only builds a plan and takes almost no time.

Expected: a table of song_a, song_b, co_count sorted by co_count descending, and a time of a few seconds on a laptop; most of it is Spark start-up and the shuffle for the join and GROUP BY, since 10,000 rows is tiny. The first run is slower than later runs (JVM warm-up). With the skeleton's single date the top count is about 11-13 and about 9,000 pairs are kept (simulated); with the two-date script, fewer.

Why it is expensive at scale: the self-join grows with the square of playlist length (10 songs give 45 pairs), which is why Spotify partitioned by week and needed hours on 2 billion playlists (P2 slide 18).

questions.q: Add a broadcast join hint for the songs dimension table and compare timings.
questions.a:
A broadcast join sends a full copy of the small table (songs: 200 rows) to every executor. Each executor joins its slice of the big table locally, so the big table is not shuffled. Hive calls this a map-side join. The hint is /*+ BROADCAST(s) */ right after SELECT.

Without the hint (and with spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold = -1 so Spark does not broadcast on its own) Spark uses a SortMergeJoin: both sides are shuffled by song_id and sorted. With the hint the plan shows BroadcastHashJoin and a BroadcastExchange for songs.

Expected: the hinted query is a little faster, but on 10,000 rows the gap is small, often well under a second and sometimes lost in noise. At real scale (billions of play events, 30M songs) avoiding the shuffle of the big table is a large saving. Note: by default Spark already broadcasts tables under 10 MB automatically, which is why the script turns that off for the comparison.

questions.q: Use EXPLAIN to print the physical plan and identify where partition pruning occurs.
questions.a:
Run EXPLAIN FORMATTED <query> or df.explain(mode="formatted"). Read the plan from the bottom (scan) up.

Where pruning shows: in the FileScan parquet node for play_events_part, the line

PartitionFilters: [isnotnull(dt#..), (dt#.. = 2024-10-01)]

That means the filter on dt is applied to directory names before any file is opened, so only the dt=2024-10-01/ folder is read and dt=2024-10-02/ is skipped. Filters on normal columns appear instead as PushedFilters (checked inside the files). Expected plan, roughly: FileScan (with PartitionFilters) then BroadcastHashJoin with BroadcastExchange(songs) then HashAggregate (partial) then Exchange then HashAggregate (final).

With the original skeleton (a temp view from an in-memory DataFrame, one date only) there are no partitions on disk, so the plan shows a scan of an in-memory/RDD source and no PartitionFilters. That is why Goal 1 writes a real partitioned table. Same idea as Hive's partition pruning in P2 slide 11 (read only dt=2024-10-01/country=BD, IN, US and skip the other 365 × 200 partitions).

maths.intro: This chapter has a handful of simple calculations: how much map-side aggregation shrinks a shuffle, how much data partition pruning skips, which bucket a row lands in, how big partitions and bucket files are, how big an ALS model is, and speed-up ratios. Each is one or two steps. All numbers below were checked in Python.

items.title: Map-side aggregation (combiner) shuffle reduction
items.symbols:
• N_rows: rows a mapper would emit without aggregation (one per input row).
  • G: number of distinct groups (GROUP BY values); with aggregation the mapper emits at most one row per group.

This is the ideal case of one mapper. With M mappers the shuffle is up to M × G rows, so the real factor is N_rows / (M × G).
items.example:
P2 slide 10: SELECT country, COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY country, 50 million rows, 200 countries.

50,000,000 / 200 = 250,000× less shuffle data.
items.practice: 120 million rows grouped by 400 regions. Reduction = 120,000,000 / 400 = 300,000×.

items.title: Partition pruning: fraction of data read
items.formula: Fraction read = P_read / P_total    (assuming equal-size partitions)
items.symbols:
• P_read: partitions matching the WHERE filter.
  • P_total: all partitions = product of the number of values of each partition column.
items.example:
P2 slide 11: table partitioned by dt (365 days) and country (200). P_total = 365 × 200 = 73,000. Query reads dt=2024-10-01 for BD, IN, US: P_read = 3.

Fraction = 3 / 73,000 ≈ 0.0041%; skipped = 72,997 partitions.

P1 slide 20: 1 month of 36 = 1/36 ≈ 2.78% read.
items.practice: 24 months × 50 countries; query one month for 2 countries. P_total = 1,200, P_read = 2. Fraction = 2 / 1,200 ≈ 0.167%.

items.title: Bucket assignment
items.symbols:
• hash(column): hash of the bucketing column; for an INT/BIGINT key in Hive this is essentially the value itself.
  • N: number of buckets from INTO N BUCKETS.
  • mod: remainder after division.

Rows with the same key always land in the same bucket number, in every table bucketed the same way, which is what makes bucket i × bucket i joins work (P1 slides 23-24).
items.example: P1 slide 24 uses 4 buckets on user_id. user_id = 98: 98 mod 4 = 2, so the row goes to bucket 2 in both sales and users.

items.title: Partition and bucket file sizing
items.formula: File size ≈ S / (P × N);   files = P × N
items.symbols:
• S: total table size.
  • P: number of partitions.
  • N: buckets per partition.

Aim for files near the HDFS block size (128 MB); far smaller means too many small files for the NameNode.
items.example: A1: S = 5 TB, 3 years × 5 countries: P = 1,095 × 5 = 5,475. Per partition = 5 TB / 5,475 ≈ 0.913 GB. N = 8: 0.913 GB / 8 ≈ 114 MB per file, 43,800 files. N = 32 would give about 28.5 MB files.
items.practice: S = 2 TB, partitioned by day for 2 years (P = 730), N = 16. File size = 2 TB / (730 × 16) = 2 TB / 11,680 ≈ 171 MB; 11,680 files.

items.title: ALS model size
items.symbols:
• U: number of users.
  • I: number of items (songs).
  • k: rank, the number of latent factors per user/item.
  • b: bytes per number (4 for a float).

Compare with the dense matrix U × I × b.
items.example: P2 slide 18: (75M + 30M) × 50 × 4 = 2.1 × 10^10 B = 21 GB. Dense matrix: 75M × 30M × 4 = 9 × 10^15 B = 9 PB. With 5,000 nodes × 64 GB (assumed) = 320 TB RAM, 21 GB fits easily.
items.practice: 10M users, 1M songs, k = 100, 4 bytes. Size = 11M × 100 × 4 = 4.4 × 10^9 B = 4.4 GB.

items.title: Speed-up and time saved
items.formula: Speed-up = T_old / T_new;   time saved % = (T_old − T_new) / T_old × 100
items.symbols:
• T_old: time before the change.
  • T_new: time after.

Use the same units for both.
items.example:
P2 slide 18: partitioning play_events by week took the query from 8 h to 2 h. Speed-up = 8 / 2 = 4×; saved = (8 − 2) / 8 = 75%.

P1 slide 26: Hive+MR 5-15 min vs Presto 5-60 s. Same-end comparisons: 300 s / 60 s = 5× and 900 s / 5 s = 180×; the slide title rounds the typical gain to 10×.
items.practice: A report drops from 2 hours to 30 minutes. Speed-up = 120 / 30 = 4×; saved = 90 / 120 = 75%.

items.title: Co-occurrence pair count
items.formula: Pairs per playlist = L(L − 1) / 2;   total pairs = number of playlists × L(L − 1) / 2;   max distinct pairs = S(S − 1) / 2
items.symbols:
• L: songs in a playlist.
  • S: songs in the catalogue.
items.example: Discussion Q1: S = 30M gives at most 4.5 × 10^14 distinct pairs. With 2B (playlist, song) rows and L = 20: 10^8 playlists × 190 = 1.9 × 10^10 pairs (about 304 GB at 16 bytes each).
items.practice: Live exercise: 1,000 playlists with about 10 songs each. Pairs = 1,000 × 10 × 9 / 2 = 45,000. (With random playlist sizes the average is a bit higher, about 50,000, which matches the simulation.) Possible distinct pairs from 200 songs = 200 × 199 / 2 = 19,900.
